links: Need grip on wet rock surfaces

skill.effect: The creature scales slick, wet surfaces without slipping, holding on strongly to navigate vertical terrain.

chains.weakness: Pads lose suction on dry, dusty rock.
observe: Pads flatten when stepping on wet stone
Shakes water off feet after rain

journal.en: They stick to the wet stone like glass beads.

plausibility.summary: Permanent humidity at the spring (D8, F15) and slick algal biofilm on tuff favor wet-adhesion or mucus-assisted grip, not Gecko-style dry van der Waals alone. Loss of grip on dry dusty rock matches how many amphibians and some lizards trade wet-surface performance for dry friction.
fixes: Permanent humidity at the spring (D8, F15) and slick algal biofilm on tuff favor wet-adhesion or mucus-assisted grip, not Gecko-style dry van der Waals alone. Loss of grip on dry dusty rock matches how many amphibians and some lizards trade wet-surface performance for dry friction.

analogues.organism: Torrent frogs (e.g. Amolops) and tree frogs use wet toe pads and mucus on submerged or spray-wetted rock; climbing salamanders (Bolitoglossa) on wet surfaces.
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

links: Need rapid acceleration to catch prey

skill.effect: It springs high into the air to snatch prey from above, extending its reach well beyond normal limits.

chains.weakness: Slow to recover balance after landing.
observe: Hind legs fold tightly before leaping
Covers vertical distance in two bounds

journal.en: A coiled spring in fur; they launch before you see them move.

plausibility.summary: Either lower mass to ~40-80 g at 8 cm, or lengthen body to ~12-15 cm at 150 g; cap vertical leap at ~0.5-0.7 m (still ~5-9 body lengths) and frame Power Leap as a snatch to low aerial insects above the pool, not rooftop height.
fixes: Either lower mass to ~40-80 g at 8 cm, or lengthen body to ~12-15 cm at 150 g; cap vertical leap at ~0.5-0.7 m (still ~5-9 body lengths) and frame Power Leap as a snatch to low aerial insects above the pool, not rooftop height.

analogues.organism: Galago/small primate and kangaroo rat hindlimb tendon recoils; frogs and fleas for high relative jump; jerboas for saltatorial acceleration.
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

links: Need photon capture during low light
Sunlight is heavily scattered by dense air (D8)

skill.effect: Its large eyes gather dim light, allowing it to spot prey clearly during twilight hours.

chains.weakness: Dazzled by sudden bright flashes or direct sun.

journal.en: Their eyes catch the last light and hold it.

plausibility.summary: Extended civil twilight (~38 min, F3) widens the crepuscular window where aerial insects are active and glare is absent. Forward-facing eyes plus tapetum lucidum increase binocular photon catch and motion detection at dusk/dawn; squinting and dazzle at midday are expected costs of a reflector-backed retina.
fixes: Extended civil twilight (~38 min, F3) widens the crepuscular window where aerial insects are active and glare is absent. Forward-facing eyes plus tapetum lucidum increase binocular photon catch and motion detection at dusk/dawn; squinting and dazzle at midday are expected costs of a reflector-backed retina.

analogues.organism: Tarsiers and galagos (forward binocular vision, nocturnal/crepuscular); domestic cat tapetum for low-light predation.
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

chains.trait: Acute hearing with mobile ear flaps
links: Insect wingbeats in dense air produce low frequencies (F4)

skill.effect: Its mobile ears swivel to catch faint wingbeats, pinpointing the location of flying prey nearby.

journal.en: They listen to the buzz before they see the wing.

plausibility.summary: Rewrite the chain: predators localize low-frequency buzz and wing rustle carried in dense still air (e.g. ~80-400 Hz band for this world's larger crepuscular insects), not insects that 'produce low frequencies because of' 1.6-bar air; keep 10 m hearing range conservative in open spring mist, shorter in storm noise.
fixes: Rewrite the chain: predators localize low-frequency buzz and wing rustle carried in dense still air (e.g. ~80-400 Hz band for this world's larger crepuscular insects), not insects that 'produce low frequencies because of' 1.6-bar air; keep 10 m hearing range conservative in open spring mist, shorter in storm noise.

analogues.organism: Fox and hare (mobile pinnae, small-prey localization); European nightjar (crepuscular insect capture, vision-heavy with auditory supplements).
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

relations.note: Small acechalunas patrol the spring edges and snatch them from cover.

secrets: Dawn chorus: they click in soft rhythms to coordinate hunting.
Albino variant: lacks dark pigment, highly sensitive to midday sun.
Fossil: found in spring-marl deposits, shows primitive toe pads.
moments: At the first pale hint of dawn, the spring pool shimmers as dozens launch from the tuff, a cloud of living sparks catching the rising insects.
